issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: John is a 53-year-old North American male who has been struggling with PTSD following a traumatic event. Married and working as a bus driver, John's life took a drastic turn when he was raped at gunpoint during his late-night shift almost two years ago. The night of the incident, John had just finished his route and was driving back to the depot when he noticed someone enter the bus through an unlocked door. Initially, he dismissed it as one last passenger who might have missed his stop. However, as the intruder approached him from behind with a gun, John's worst fears were realized. The terror he felt that night has become a recurring nightmare, replaying like a film whenever he closes his eyes or tries to relax. Since then, feeling tired and exhausted is no longer just about being physically drained; it triggers intense memories of the helplessness he experienced during the assault. As a bus driver, John often encounters passengers who board late or are visibly distressed, which makes him feel anxious about driving with others. The sounds of footsteps in the aisle or doors closing loudly evoke vivid auditory reminders of that night. John has become hyper-vigilant and often feels like his body is tainted by what happened to it. When he remembers the event, the terror and shame return with such intensity that he struggles to differentiate between past and present. He describes these memories as a film that replays over and over, leaving him feeling both exposed and vulnerable. Over time, John's trust in others has diminished significantly. He had come to believe that people can't be trusted, especially those who might have the opportunity to isolate him again. This mistrust extends to his marriage; he finds it difficult to open up about his fears and experiences with his wife, leading to a growing distance between them. John's work as a bus driver has become increasingly challenging. He avoids routes that are less frequented or where passengers might be alone on the bus, often altering his schedule without informing his supervisors. This behavior has led to missed shifts and confrontations at work, further isolating him from colleagues who see his actions as irresponsible. His loss of faith in people and life itself has deepened his sense of despair. He feels that he can no longer trust anyone or anything, including the idea of a higher power that once gave him solace. The shame associated with what happened to his body is particularly burdensome, making it hard for him to engage in physical activities or even maintain his usual hygiene routines. What frightens John most is the fear of these memories and triggers overwhelming him entirely. He worries about losing control at work or home, unable to cope with the constant reminders that follow him everywhere. Despite this, he recognizes that continuing to avoid his fears will only lead to further isolation and deterioration in both his professional and personal life. Finally, John decided to seek help after a recent incident where his anxiety during a shift caused him to drive recklessly, narrowly avoiding an accident. This close call made him realize the need for intervention before things spiral out of control completely. He is hopeful that with support, he can regain some sense of normalcy and trust in life again.
